caitlynAuthorisation.about: The entity types @permission may name, read by the CaitlynPermissions lint rule. Every entity type is checked through the app's role grants (src/constants/roles/entities.ts); `grantTypes` lists the grants a role can hold on it, and @permission's `level` must be one of them. The permission names themselves come from permissions.json, which is generated.

agents.description: An agent; version access is checked on the agent's version access grant.

clients.description: An organisation-scoped grant ('own' or '*'), meaning where the role is held, never a record identifier.

conversations.description: A conversation. Checked through role grants like every other entity, so shared conversations need no second mechanism. Owner is a native grant type: the person or client that creates a conversation is given the owner grant on it, which includes every other level.

policy-sets.description: A policy. The entity type keeps the app's existing name, like the OAuth scope.

uploads.description: An upload slot. Not shared through role grants: the person or client that reserved it holds the owner grant, and anyone else gets 404.

Why the read is sensitive, for the audit log's readers.

A read whose data is sensitive (personal data, an export, a transcript). It is audited like a
write: the `attempted` event is awaited before the data goes out, the request is refused with
503 when no audit event can be recorded, and the event is kept in the audit table. Writes are
always audited this way and do not carry the trait. Every other read publishes only its
outcome, and is served even when that event cannot be published.

The member may be named in the update's `clear` list, which returns it to its default.
Naming any other member in `clear` is refused with 400 `VALIDATION_FAILED`.

A path of lower camel case words, dotted when nested, for example "conversations" or
"agents.options". Absent: for a bound operation, the place the resource model gives it; for an
unbound one, the top of the client.
The method name, lower camel case, for example "send".

Where an operation appears in the SDKs' clients, where the resource model does not give the right
place or name (PROTOCOL.md, section 10). Python snake-cases the name.

For an operation bound to a resource, `namespace` is a path relative to where the operation would
otherwise appear: the resource's scope for an instance operation, its collection for a collection
operation. For example CreateConversation, bound to a version, has namespace "conversations" and
name "create" (`agent.live.conversations.create(…)`). For an operation bound to no resource,
`namespace` is absolute, for example "agents.options" (`caitlyn.agents.options.models()`), and
absent for a method at the top of the client (`caitlyn.me()`).
A namespace never starts `core.`: the generators place `@lowLevel` operations under `core` themselves.

The stable problem `code` values an error shape carries. One error shape per HTTP status
(PROTOCOL.md, lint rule 1), so every code for that status is listed here. Codes are
UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, at most 63 characters, and never renamed once shipped.
The job.

The operation estimates what another operation, the job, would do and cost, from the same
arguments. The SDKs place it beside the job (`kb.fields.fillIn.estimate(keys)`). Every member of the
estimate's input is a member of the job's input with the same target, except `file` or
`documents`, which describe the files a job would take as uploads (CaitlynEstimate).
Every caller who may read the resource the stream belongs to.

Every caller who may read the resource the stream belongs to, as for `public`, but the event
may still change before it is generally available.
Only callers with a debug permission.
Only when the setting that controls it is on (for example `deniedDocuments` on a version).
Who receives an event on a stream. Every member of an `@sseEvents` union declares exactly one.

The filters a List accepts: each key is an item member (dots for nested members, for example
"target.type") and each value lists the operators allowed on it. An undeclared field or
operator is refused with 400 `UNKNOWN_FILTER`.

The member names the resource whose scope the operation is also offered on: called on that scope,
the member is filled from the scope's identifier. One operation then serves several scopes, for
example GetAccess on a knowledge base, on `kb.folders(path)` (filling `folder`) and on
`kb.documents(id)` (filling `document`).
Why a caller may leave `If-Match` out.

The operation binds `If-Match`, but does not require it: without one, the change applies to the
resource as it is. Allowed only with a reason, and only on the operations Sam approved on
17 November 2026 (the draft's update, replace and save, publishing, access, starting a batch,
adding a document version, a field's update and resolving a batch item), which a validator test
pins; every other write that binds `If-Match` requires it.

The operation issues or revokes credentials, so no token may call it: its permission belongs to
no scope, and any token is refused with 403 `NOT_AVAILABLE_TO_CREDENTIALS`. A credential that
could mint credentials would escape its own revocation.
The watch: an operation with `@sseEvents` whose first event is a snapshot.
The watch's input member the scope's identifier fills. Absent: the watch is the scope's own.

The call cancels the work it follows: its wait() returns the thing once that work has stopped,
and the job it cancelled ending `cancelled` is not a failure (conformance case
wait.cancel-returns).

The work the operation starts, or the work on the resource, is followed through this watch: the
generators give the returned scope, or the resource's scope, `watch()` and `wait()` built on it
(PROTOCOL.md, section 16). `filter` names the watch's input member that the scope's identifier
fills, so the watch carries only that thing's events.

The resource, or operation, is a building block that the SDKs' higher-level helpers are made
from, such as the upload slot behind every file helper. The SDKs place its client methods under the
`core` namespace (`client.core.uploads.reserve(…)`), so the everyday surface stays small and the
building blocks stay reachable. The generators place every operation of a `@lowLevel` resource,
and every `@lowLevel` operation, under `core`, taking its scopes' identifiers as arguments
(`caitlyn.core.ingestion.completeUploads(kbId, batchId, itemIds)`).
Why no audit event is needed.
The operation is not audited. Meant only for operations such as the health check.
Why no permission applies.

The credential types allowed to call the operation, as on `@permission`. Absent means
people only.

The operation checks no permission and needs no scope of its own: any signed-in caller of the
listed credential types may call it. Unlike `@optionalAuth`, a credential is still required. It
is allowed on two kinds of read only:

- an operation that describes the caller's own credential, such as `GET /v3/me`, which takes no
  input and is not a List;
- an event stream (`@sseEvents`) with no path labels, such as the workspace event stream: the
  server checks each event against the caller's own permission and scope for that event's subject
  before sending it, as a read of that subject would. A stream that names records in a filter
  (the workspace stream's `conversationIds`) relies on that check, which it records with a
  reasoned `@suppress` of CaitlynPermissions.NamesRecords.

Anything that names or lists records declares the `@permission` that guards them. This is the
standard trait for "signed in, no scope needed"; a new use needs the `smithy/` code owners'
approval, like `@noAudit`.
The permission, for example "agents.update".

More permissions the caller must hold as well as `action`, where v2 requires several at once
(a paid job needs `knowledge-bases.ingestions.update` beside `knowledge-bases.update`). Each
maps to its own scope, and a credential needs every one.

The record the grant check follows. Required on every operation that takes a record
identifier.

On an operation whose entity is a conversation: also check the agent and version the
conversation was started on, which the server reads from the conversation, as v2's chat turns
do (nativeChatRouteGuards.ts). The caller needs the agent grant at `level` on that agent and,
for a version other than `live`, the agent's version access grant, so revoking either stops
the caller chatting in conversations already started.

Checks that replace `action`, `alsoActions` and `entity` when the input names something the
operation's own check does not cover. The first variant with any of its `members` present
applies; with none present, the operation's own check does. PutAccess on a knowledge base
changes its role grants, but on a folder or document only that record's readers.
On a List: the entity type whose grants filter the list inside the database query.

The credential types allowed to call the operation. Absent means people only (a browser
session, or a token acting as one person). Machine clients and guest tokens must be listed.

`primary` on operations that only the organisation's primary workspace serves; elsewhere
they are refused with 403 `PRIMARY_WORKSPACE_REQUIRED`.

The permission an operation checks, in the app's existing permission vocabulary
(`AUTH_SETTINGS`). The OAuth scope is derived from it by the scope catalogue, never written by
hand. The generated wrapper checks, in order: caller type (403), primary workspace (403), the
permission (403), then the entity, version and document checks (404).

The operation reserves an upload slot: its input has fileName, contentType, byteSize and
sha256 (base64 SHA-256), and its output has uploadUrl, uploadMethod and requiredHeaders.
Generators may emit an `uploads.create(file)` helper that computes the checksum and sends the

The collection's path under the parent scope, lower camel case and dotted when nested, for
example "ingestion.batches" (`kb.ingestion.batches(batchId)`) or "history". Default: the resource

The scope method's name in Go and Rust, which cannot call a value that also has fields, for

The resource is a scope in the SDKs' clients: called with its identifier, it gives an object that
every operation on the resource hangs off (`caitlyn.knowledgeBases(kbId).documents(documentId)`).
Every resource with an identifier of its own is a scope, so the trait is needed only to change the
names the resource model gives. A resource with no identifier beyond its parent's (a singleton, such
as an agent's draft) is a scope reached as a property (`agent.draft`), named by `collection`; when a
sibling resource has an alias of the same name (`@scopeAliases`), the two are one scope.

Named scopes of the resource with a fixed identifier value, offered beside the scope taking an
identifier. On an agent's VersionResource, `draft` and `live` give `agent.draft` and `agent.live`
beside `agent.versions(name)`. Each alias may leave out operations that make no sense for it.

The Caitlyn release that introduced an operation or member, for example "5.120.0".

Authors write `@since("next")`. The release step replaces every "next" with the release number
when the model is published (smithy/scripts/stamp-since.sh), so a hand-typed number can never
name the wrong release. The SDK refuses to call an operation, or send a member, that is newer
than the server's `Caitlyn-Api-Version`.
Item members the caller may sort by.

traits.smithy.api#documentation:
Publishes a version: live then points at it.

Called on `draft`, it first keeps the draft as a new version named `name`, then points live at it,
so live always names a version. The publish permission alone is enough for both: publishing the
draft needs no permission to create versions, which SaveDraftVersion needs to keep a version
without making it live. Called on a named version, it points live at that version, which
rolls back when live pointed at it before: nothing is copied, and the history entry's `kind` is
`rollback`. Versions never change once made, so live answers exactly as the version it names.

Two publishes cannot silently overwrite each other when the caller says what it expects live to
be: `expectedLive` names the version (or `none` before the first publish), or `If-Match` carries
live's ETag. Either, when stale, is refused with 412; with neither, the publish applies to live as
it is. Returns live, the version published, and the history entry the publish wrote.

traits.smithy.api#documentation:
Sets who may use a knowledge base, or who may read a folder or a document in it.

`If-Match` is optional. Without it the write is unconditional and the last writer wins, which is
safe because the caller sends the whole list. With it, access that changed since is refused with
412.

Without `folder` or `document`, send `roles`: the roles sent become the whole list. With `folder` or
`document`, send `readers`; `kind: inherit` makes it follow its folder again. The knowledge base's
role grants are set only without a target, under the knowledge base's own permission, as v2's
knowledge base permissions route sets them, so `roles` with `folder` or `document`, `readers`
without one, and both `folder` and `document` are refused with 400 `VALIDATION_FAILED`. The root folder
(`folder=/`) holds the readers every other folder falls back to, so `inherit` is refused there
with 400 `VALIDATION_FAILED`. Applying readers to
the passages a folder or document holds continues after the response; the returned access says
what is set, and the knowledge base's watch shows the work.

Setting `roles` is refused in two cases, as in v2. A caller may give a role only a grant it
could make itself: any other is refused with 403 `PERMISSION_DENIED`. And a grant that is not
safe for guests, given to a role that guests or anonymous visitors use, is refused with 422
`RBAC_NOT_GUEST_SAFE`. Only the grants being added are judged, so a grant the role already holds
never blocks an unrelated change. Both checks are made by the server on the roles sent.

traits.smithy.api#documentation:
Starts a planned ingestion batch, and returns the upload policy for the items that need bytes.

`If-Match` is optional. Without it, the batch starts as it stands; with it, a batch that changed
since that ETag is refused with 412. A stale plan is planned again first. Each item's write is then checked and
claimed: a new document is reserved at its path, and an existing one is protected by its own
version, so a document that changed since the plan becomes a `changed_since_plan` conflict. An item

its `objectKey`, then report them with CompleteIngestionBatchUploads.

files delete permission, and each item that moves one, or adds a new version of one, for the files
update permission, and the token's scope covers it too. An item that fails the check is marked
`failed` with `PERMISSION_DENIED` and the rest carry on. This holds whether the batch starts
through StartIngestionBatch or by itself under `start: when_planned`, so the permission is checked
per item, not once on the call.

caller closes the stream. An answer whose stream ended moments before the watch opened may still
be delivered, from its `message.started` event; match answers on your own message ID.

from its start, so it shows the answer so far. An answer too long for the replay buffer cannot be
replayed: the watch sends `stream.reset` instead, then the answers after it. Read the turn with
ListMessages once it ends.

With `Last-Event-ID`, it resumes from the event after that one, so a dropped connection loses
nothing; the SDKs use this to re-attach to `SendMessage`, and to reconnect a dropped watch. When
the answer that event belongs to has ended, or can no longer be replayed, the watch sends
`stream.reset` with a new cursor instead, then carries on. Each answer ends with
`message.completed` or `message.failed`, which end that answer but not the stream, so
helpers watch for the event they need and then close.

an error. To wait for something your own call will cause, open the stream first, then make the
call.

with its content, in the same structures as the conversation's own stream.
